chunks: As for what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥasan ibn Maḥbūb, from al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Razīn, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I said to Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام: How is it that ghusl is made obligatory upon a woman when she sees in sleep that a man is having intercourse with her in her private part, yet ghusl is not made obligatory upon her if he has intercourse with her outside the private part while awake and she emits fluid?

He said: 'Because she saw in her dream that the man was having intercourse with her in her private part, so ghusl became obligatory upon her. But in the other case, he only had intercourse with her outside the private part, so ghusl did not become obligatory upon her because he did not insert it. And if he had inserted it while awake, ghusl would have become obligatory upon her, whether she emitted fluid or did not emit fluid.'
So the explanation of this report as well is the same as what we mentioned regarding the first report; it indicates that equally.

key_terms.دُونَ الْفَرْجِ: outside the private part; indicating non-penetrative contact
key_terms.فِي النَّوْمِ: in sleep; referring to the dream state
key_terms.فِي الْيَقَظَةِ: in wakefulness; referring to the waking state
key_terms.فِي فَرْجِهَا: in her private part; indicating vaginal penetration

ai.seo_question: When does ghusl become obligatory for a woman according to this hadith from Tahdhīb al-Aḥkām?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses the legal ruling of ghusl in relation to janabah for a woman in cases of dream intercourse and physical contact outside vaginal penetration. It distinguishes between the ruling based on perceived intercourse in a dream and actual waking penetration, clarifying that ghusl becomes obligatory with penetration whether emission occurs or not.
